summary:
The Last 72 Hours is a browser-native, first-person 3D lunar survival simulator designed to train the Artemis generation (ages 7–12) using authentic NASA science. Set at Aurora Outpost on the Lunar South Pole, players step into the role of Mission Operator during the final 72 hours before a SpaceX Starship HLS resupply craft lands.

Instead of passively memorizing textbook facts, young learners experience hands-on space engineering through a 3-step loop: consulting crew field guides powered by NASA datasets (BVAD, DONKI, LRO CRaTER, ECLSS, and OSDR), piloting a remote EVA rover to salvage parts while avoiding high-radiation zones, and executing exact repair sequences across eight interconnected life-support subsystems.

By turning abstract space hazards—low-angle 3° sunlight, abrasive lunar regolith, CO₂ buildup, and Solar Particle Events—into visible cause-and-effect trade-offs, our project bridges the gap between complex NASA data and youth STEM literacy.
details:
The Last 72 Hours is an interactive first-person 3D lunar habitat simulation built on a modular TypeScript engine and Three.js. Spanning 9 shifts across 72 hours, the simulation models eight interconnected life-support subsystems—Power, Oxygen, Water Recovery, CO₂ Scrubbing, Thermal Control, Hydroponic Botany, Crew Health, and Radiation Shielding.

Rather than guessing multiple-choice answers, players follow a structured 3-step NASA engineering workflow:

  1. Consult Crew & NASA Guides: Interact with Station Commander AI (inspired by NASA's Astrobee), Engineer Sam, and Dr. Maya to study concise scientific principles (≤12 words per prompt for ages 7–12).
  2. Pilot the EVA Rover: Operate a remote rover with directional headlights across low-visibility lunar terrain to recover spare components while avoiding high-radiation (RAD) zones.
  3. Execute 3-Step Technical Repairs & Resource Trade-Offs: Assemble components in the exact engineering order (e.g., depressurize → replace filter → reboot), then allocate scarce resources (such as prioritizing emergency life support over greenhouse grow lights). At the end of 72 hours, the Astronaut Science Journal debriefs players by comparing their top decisions against real historical NASA missions.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • For Young Learners (Ages 7–12): Transforms abstract space science into active systems thinking, teaching why every drop of water, watt of power, and millimeter of shielding matters beyond Earth.
  • For Educators & Classrooms: Provides a zero-installation, browser-native STEM tool complete with an In-Game NASA Science Reference Library (SCI-01 to SCI-11) that clearly separates real NASA metrics from gameplay abstractions.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Core Stack: TypeScript, React, Three.js (3D rendering), Tailwind CSS, and HTML5.
  • Audio & Optimization: Procedural Web Audio API synthesizer (adaptive space ambience & alert SFX) and dynamic Device Pixel Ratio (DPR) scaling.
  • Development & Media Tools: Google AI Studio (code scaffolding & prototyping), Cloudflare Pages (web deployment), Clipchamp (demo video editing), and Gamma (pitch deck).

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

  • Child-Centered Cognitive Design: Strictly capped dialogue lengths, visual cause-and-effect feedback (wilting crops, dimming lights, red storm strobes), and safe failure states (incorrect repair steps trigger temporary faults with instant scientific explanations rather than frustrating game-overs).
  • Hardware & Language Accessibility: Built an Auto-Adaptive Low-Graphics Mode so older school computers run smoothly at 60 FPS, alongside full English / Vietnamese bilingual support.
  • Astronomical & Medical Accuracy: Positioned the Sun at a realistic 3° low elevation angle on the Lunar South Pole horizon and grounded radiation protection in hydrogen-rich water walls and regolith shielding.
